sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in Buffalo, New York
Wikipedia GeoSearch, 2.5 km around downtown Buffalo (42.8864, -78.8784)
Category:Buildings and structures in Buffalo, New York

stops.name: Buffalo City Hall
stops.description: A 32-story Art Deco slab finished in 1931, still the seat of city government, with a free observation deck on the 28th floor open on weekdays.

stops.name: McKinley Monument
stops.description: A 96-foot marble obelisk ringed by lions, raised in 1907 to William McKinley, who was shot at Buffalo's Pan-American Exposition six years earlier.

stops.name: Prudential (Guaranty) Building
stops.description: Louis Sullivan and Dankmar Adler's 1896 terra-cotta skyscraper, a National Historic Landmark whose ground-floor interpretive center is open during business hours.

stops.name: St. Paul's Cathedral
stops.description: Richard Upjohn called this 1851 Gothic Revival cathedral his best work; it burned in 1888 and was rebuilt inside its surviving stone walls.

stops.name: Ellicott Square Building
stops.description: When Daniel Burnham's firm finished it in 1896 it was the largest office building in the world, and its glass-roofed courtyard is still open to walk through.

stops.name: Old Post Office
stops.description: A Gothic Revival federal post office opened in 1901, gargoyles and all, that has housed SUNY Erie's City Campus since 1981.

stops.name: Lafayette Square
stops.description: The city block where Lafayette himself spoke in 1825, now centered on an 85-foot Civil War Soldiers and Sailors Monument dedicated by Grover Cleveland.

stops.name: Liberty Building
stops.description: Look up: three 36-foot replicas of the Statue of Liberty, sculpted in 1925, stand on and over this neo-classical tower and are lit at night.

stops.name: Hotel Lafayette
stops.description: The French Renaissance masterwork of Louise Blanchard Bethune, the first professional woman architect in the United States, restored in 2012 and open again as a hotel.

stops.name: Electric Tower
stops.description: A 1912 tower modeled on the Pan-American Exposition's Electric Tower, and the spot where Buffalo drops its ball on New Year's Eve.

stops.name: Buffalo Savings Bank
stops.description: Locals navigate by the Gold Dome: 13,500 terra-cotta tiles under gold leaf, capping a Beaux-Arts bank that opened in 1901 and is still a bank branch.

stops.name: Shea's Performing Arts Center
stops.description: A 1926 movie palace by Rapp and Rapp, saved from demolition in the 1970s and still running touring Broadway shows.

stops.name: Colored Musicians Club
stops.description: Founded in 1935 by Buffalo's all-Black musicians' union local, it is the last club of its kind in the country and still hosts a Sunday jam session upstairs.

stops.name: Michigan Street Baptist Church
stops.description: Built by its congregation in 1845, this sandstone church sheltered freedom seekers a short walk from the Canadian border and still offers docent tours.

stops.name: Buffalo and Erie County Naval & Military Park
stops.description: Three decommissioned warships sit in the water at Canalside, among them USS The Sullivans, named for five brothers lost together at Guadalcanal.

note: First run for Buffalo. Downtown is unusually dense in NRHP listings, so every stop here has its own Wikipedia article with coordinates, and every street address was confirmed against an independent source before the ZIP was looked up. Two ZIPs come straight from Wikipedia infoboxes (Shea's 14202, Electric Tower 14203); the rest are lookups against venue or listing pages. The loop is closer to 1.5 miles than 1: the core runs Niagara Square to Lafayette Square to Fountain Plaza along Main St, with two spurs a human may want to trim - Canalside and the Naval Park about half a mile south, and the Michigan Street pair (Colored Musicians Club, Michigan Street Baptist Church) about half a mile east on the African American Heritage Corridor. Two stops use a square rather than a numbered street for the address, which is how the NRHP rows give them: McKinley Monument (Niagara Sq) and Lafayette Square (Lafayette Sq). Dropped: Erie County Savings Bank and the Larkin Administration Building, both long demolished; the Rand Building and the 1964 Central Library, cut only to hold the batch at 15 and both worth revisiting; Kleinhans Music Hall and the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site, real and verified but too far out of the walkable core. Also skipped Metro Rail stations, historic districts, and neighborhood articles, which are areas rather than places to stand in front of.
